## Why trace a layout?

Most graph-layout functions return only the final coordinate matrix. That is
enough for plotting, but it hides the most useful diagnostic information:

- how the multiscale hierarchy opened,
- whether the geometry stabilized gradually or abruptly,
- whether a parameter setting improved edge-length regularity or only moved the
  final picture around,
- and whether a weighted solve is actually getting closer to the intended
  metric geometry.

The `trace.grip()` API makes those questions visible through the same metric
choice as `grip()`:

- `trace.grip(metric = "hop")` for combinatorial layouts,
- `trace.grip(metric = "edge_length")` for edge-length geometry-aware layouts.

```{r}
library(grip)
source(system.file('scripts','vignette-views.R',package='grip'),local=TRUE)
```

## A first combinatorial trace

The example below traces a planar recursive triangle. Its nested holes make
the multiscale construction visible. Using
`trace = "level"` keeps the vignette readable by recording the coarse
initialization, the start of each new level, and the final layout.

```{r}
mesh.edges <- edges.sierpinski.triangle(4)

mesh.trace <- trace.grip(
  mesh.edges,
  n = max(mesh.edges),
  dim = 2,
  preset = "carpet",
  rounds = 48,
  final.rounds = 96,
  trace = "level",
  diagnostics = "light",
  seed = 1
)

knitr::kable(mesh.trace$meta)
knitr::kable(mesh.trace$diagnostics[, c(
  "frame",
  "edge.length.cv",
  "median.edge.length",
  "sampled.nonedge.sep.ratio"
)], digits = 3)
```

```{r trace-view, echo=FALSE}
htmltools::tagList(lapply(seq_along(mesh.trace$frames), function(i) {
  z <- mesh.trace$frames[[i]]
  active <- stats::complete.cases(z)
  e <- mesh.edges[active[mesh.edges[,1]] & active[mesh.edges[,2]],,drop=FALSE]
  ids <- integer(nrow(z)); ids[active] <- seq_len(sum(active))
  e <- matrix(ids[e],ncol=2)
  z <- z[active,,drop=FALSE]
  if (ncol(z)==2L) z <- cbind(z,0)
  htmltools::tagList(
    htmltools::tags$h3(paste('Recorded stage',i,'of',length(mesh.trace$frames))),
    ivue::plot3D.plain(z,layers=list(ivue::layer3D.edges(e)),
      axes=FALSE,aspect='equal',width=900,height=420,
      description=paste('Stage',i,':',sum(active),'active vertices. Original planar coordinates.'))
  )
}))
```

Each recorded stage has an ivue viewer showing its active vertices and edges.
Drag to rotate or scroll to zoom. Original planar coordinates are retained at
z = 0; each viewer fits its own bounds, so apparent size across stages is not
a measure of expansion.


The two most useful tables are:

- `meta`, which explains where each frame came from,
- `diagnostics`, which tracks simple quality signals frame by frame.

## Level traces versus round traces

When you need more detail, `trace = "round"` records intermediate refinement
rounds within each active level.

```{r}
mesh.trace.round <- trace.grip(
  mesh.edges,
  n = max(mesh.edges),
  dim = 2,
  preset = "carpet",
  rounds = 6,
  final.rounds = 8,
  trace = "round",
  trace.every = 4,
  diagnostics = "light",
  seed = 1
)

data.frame(
  trace_mode = c("level", "round"),
  n.frames = c(length(mesh.trace$frames), length(mesh.trace.round$frames))
)
```

Use:

- `trace = "level"` for most reporting and teaching,
- `trace = "round"` when you are diagnosing a tuning issue.

## Read changes over the trace

```{r diagnostic-curve, echo=FALSE}
plot(mesh.trace$diagnostics$frame,mesh.trace$diagnostics$edge.length.cv,
  type='b',pch=16,col='#1769AA',xlab='Recorded frame',ylab='Edge-length variation')
```

Early frames contain only the active coarse vertices. Read changes in the
score together with the stage and active graph; adjacent frames may not score
identical vertex sets. Level traces show insertion stages; round traces show
more of the refinement within each stage. They are different sampling schedules.

For a weighted graph, use `trace.grip(metric='edge_length', ...)` with its
lengths. The [weighted guide](weighted-grip-intro.html) explains this metric.
Detailed construction animations and their reproduction commands are described
in the [asset guide](https://github.com/pgajer/grip/blob/main/tools/README.md#readme-and-showcase-assets).

## Trace objects are analysis objects

A trace object is more than a list of pictures. It can support:

- frame-by-frame diagnostics,
- manual inspection of where a solve destabilizes,
- teaching demonstrations of the multiscale hierarchy,
- and regression checks for future algorithm changes.

The most useful components are:

- `final`: the final coordinate matrix,
- `frames`: the stored coordinate frames,
- `meta`: frame provenance,
- `diagnostics`: per-frame metrics,
- `lgkk.polish`: optional post-layout LGKK result when enabled as an advanced
  experimental refinement step.

## Practical guidance

- Start with `trace = "level"` and `diagnostics = "light"`.
- Use `trace = "round"` only when you need finer-grained diagnostics.
- Supply `target.coords` when a meaningful geometric target exists.
- Prefer weighted traces for weighted graph families; they are much more
  interpretable than tracing the combinatorial solver on a graph with
  nontrivial edge lengths.
